title: Subs. by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s.12 for "two years" (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). Explanation I
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 1: Subs. by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s.12 for "two years" (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). Explanation I
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

The expression “law in force” in this article shall include 
a law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the 
territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not 
previously repealed, notwithstanding that it or parts of it may not be then in 
operation either at all or in particular areas. 
Explanation II.—Any law passed or made by a Legislature or other 
competent authority in the territory of India which immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution had extra-territorial effect as well as effect 
in the territory of India shall, subject to any such adaptations and modifications 
as aforesaid, continue to have such extra-territorial effect. 
Explanation III.—Nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing 
any temporary law in force beyond the date fixed for its expiration or the date on 
which it would have expired if this Constitution had not come into force. 
Explanation IV.—An Ordinance promulgated by the Governor of a 
Province under section 88 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and in force 
immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless 
withdrawn by the Governor of the corresponding State earlier, cease to operate 
at the expiration of six weeks from the first meeting after such commencement 
of the Legislative Assembly of that State functioning under clause (1) of article 
382, and nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing any such 
Ordinance in force beyond the said period.

title: Power of the President to adapt laws
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 372A: Power of the President to adapt laws
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

(1) For the purposes 
of bringing the provisions of any law in force in India or in any part thereof, 
immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh 
Amendment) Act, 1956, into accord with the provisions of this Constitution as 
amended by that Act, the President may by order made before the first day of 
November, 1957, make such adaptations and modifications of the law, whether 
by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and provide 
that the law shall, as from such date as may be specified in the order, have effect 
subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such adaptation or 
modification shall not be questioned in any court of law. 
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall be deemed to prevent a competent 
Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law 
adapted or modified by the President under the said clause. 
 
1. Ins. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 23 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956). 
 See the Adaptation of Laws Order of 1956 and 1957.

title: Power of President to make order in respect of persons under preventive detention in certain cases
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 373: Power of President to make order in respect of persons under preventive detention in certain cases
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

Until provision is made by Parliament 
under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the 
commencement of this Constitution, whichever is earlier, the said article shall 
have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof 
there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to an 
order made by the President.

title: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council - Clause (1)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 374: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (1): (1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in respect 
of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in respect 
of the Judges of the Supreme Court.

title: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council - Clause (2)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 374: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (2): (2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.

title: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council - Clause (3)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 374: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (3): (3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and any 
order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after the 
commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it were 
an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the jurisdiction 
conferred on such Court by this Constitution.

title: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council - Clause (4)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 374: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (4): (4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.

title: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council - Clause (5)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 374: Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (5): (5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

title: Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject to the provisions of the Constitution
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 375: Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject to the provisions of the Constitution
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

All courts of civil, criminal and revenue 
jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and ministerial, 
throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their respective 
functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.

title: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts - Clause (1)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 376: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (1): (1) Notwithstanding 
anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any Province 
holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, 
unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges 
of the High Court in the corresponding State, and shall thereupon be entitled to 
such salaries and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and 
pension as are provided for under article 221 in respect of the Judges of such 
High Court. Any such Judge shall, notwithstanding that he is not a citizen of 
India, be eligible for appointment as Chief Justice of such High Court, or as Chief 
Justice or other Judge of any other High Court.

title: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts - Clause (2)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 376: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (2): (2) The Judges of a High Court in any Indian State corresponding to any 
State specified in Part B of the First Schedule holding office immediately before 
the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the State so 
specified and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 217 
but subject to the proviso to clause (1) of that article, continue to hold office until 
the expiration of such period as the President may by order determine.

title: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts - Clause (3)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 376: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (3): (3) In this article, the expression “Judge” does not include an acting Judge 
or an additional Judge.

title: Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 377: Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

The 
Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of 
this Constitution shall, unless he has elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon 
be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and 
pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office 
until the expiration of his term of office as determined under the provisions which 
were applicable to him immediately before such commencement. 
 
 
1. Added by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s. 13 (w.e.f. 18-6-1951).

title: Provisions as to Public Service Commissions - Clause (1)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 378: Provisions as to Public Service Commissions
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (1): (1) The members 
of the Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India holding office 
immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they 
have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the 
Public Service Commission for the Union and shall, notwithstanding anything in 
clauses (1) and (2) of article 316 but subject to the proviso to clause (2) of that 
article, continue to hold office until the expiration of their term of office as 
determined under the rules which were applicable immediately before such 
commencement to such members.

title: Provisions as to Public Service Commissions - Clause (2)
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 378: Provisions as to Public Service Commissions
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
Clause (2): (2) The Members of a Public Service Commission of a Province or of a 
Public Service Commission serving the needs of a group of Provinces holding 
office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they 
have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the Public 
Service Commission for the corresponding State or the members of the Joint State 
Public Service Commission serving the needs of the corresponding States, as the 
case may be, and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 
316 but subject to the proviso to clause (2) of that article, continue to hold office 
until the expiration of their term of office as determined under the rules which were 
applicable immediately before such commencement to such members.

title: Special provision as to duration of Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 378A: Special provision as to duration of Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

Notwithstanding anything contained in article 172, the 
Legislative Assembly of the State of Andhra Pradesh as constituted under the 
provisions of sections 28 and 29 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, shall, 
unless sooner dissolved, continue for a period of five years from the date referred 
to in the said section 29 and no longer and the expiration of the said period shall 
operate as a dissolution of that Legislative Assembly.

title: Power of the President to remove difficulties
part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
text:
Article 392: Power of the President to remove difficulties
Part: Part XXI - Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

(1) The President 
may, for the purpose of removing any difficulties, particularly in relation to the 
transition from the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, to the 
provisions of this Constitution, by order direct that this Constitution shall, during 
such period as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to such 
adaptations, whether by way of modification, addition or omission, as he may 
deem to be necessary or expedient: 
Provided that no such order shall be made after the first meeting of 
Parliament duly constituted under Chapter II of Part V. 
(2) Every order made under clause (1) shall be laid before Parliament. 
(3) The powers conferred on the President by this article, by article 324, by 
clause (3) of article 367 and by article 391 shall, before the commencement of this 
Constitution, be exercisable by the Governor-General of the Dominion of India. 
 
 
 
PART XXII 
 
 
 
 
India.

Article 393: Short title
Part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals

This Constitution may be called the Constitution of

title: Commencement
part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals
text:
Article 394: Commencement
Part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals

This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the 
remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-
sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the 
commencement of this Constitution.

title: Authoritative text in the Hindi language
part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals
text:
Article 394A: Authoritative text in the Hindi language
Part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals

(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and 
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably. 
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.

title: Repeals
part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals
text:
Article 395: Repeals
Part: Part XXII - Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals

The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed. 
 
1. Ins. by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987, s. 2 (w.e.f. 9-12-1987). 
2. Art 394A, Ins. by s. 3, ibid. (w.e.f. 9-12-1987).

Fifth Schedule - Part 1

[Article 244(1)] 
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and 
Scheduled Tribes 
PART A 
GENERAL 
1. Interpretation.—In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the expression “State” 1 does not include the 2[States of Assam 
3[, 4[Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.]]] 
2. Executive power of a State in Scheduled Areas.—Subject to the 
provisions of this Schedule, the executive power of a State extends to the 
Scheduled Areas therein. 
3. Report by the Governor 5 to the President regarding the 
administration of Scheduled Areas.—The Governor 5 of each State having 
Scheduled Areas therein shall annually, or whenever so required by the President, 
make a report to the President regarding the administration of the Scheduled 
Areas in that State and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the 
giving of directions to the State as to the administration of the said areas. 
PART B 
ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF SCHEDULED AREAS AND 
SCHEDULED TRIBES 
4. Tribes Advisory Council.—(1) There shall be established in each 
State having Scheduled Areas therein and, if the President so directs, also in any 
State having Scheduled Tribes but not Scheduled Areas therein, a Tribes 
Advisory Council consisting of not more than twenty members of whom, as

Tenth Schedule - Part 1

[Articles 102(2) and 191(2)] 
Provisions as to disqualification on ground of defection 
1. Interpretation.—In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise requires,— 
(a) "House" means either House of Parliament or the Legislative 
Assembly or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature of a State; 
(b) "legislature party", in relation to a member of a House 
belonging to any political party in accordance with the provisions of 
paragraph 2 or 2 paragraph 4, means the group consisting of all the 
members of that House for the time being belonging to that political party 
in accordance with the said provisions; 
(c) "original political party", in relation to a member of a House, 
means the political party to which he belongs for the purposes of sub-
paragraph (1) of paragraph 2; 
(d) "paragraph" means a paragraph of this Schedule. 
2. Disqualification on ground of defection.—(1) Subject to the 
provisions of 3[paragraphs 4 and 5], a member of a House belonging to any 
political party shall be disqualified for being a member of the House— 
(a) if he has voluntarily given up his membership of such political 
party; or 
(b) if he votes or abstains from voting in such House contrary to 
any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs or by any 
person or authority authorised by it in this behalf, without obtaining, in 
either case, the prior permission of such political party, person or authority 
and such voting or abstention has not been condoned by such political 
party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of such voting 
or abstentio

and such voting or abstention has not been condoned by such political 
party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of such voting 
or abstention.

(a) an elected member of a House shall be deemed to belong to the 
political party, if any, by which he was set up as a candidate for election 
as such member; 
(b) a nominated member of a House shall,—

5. Exemption.—Notwithstanding anything contained in this Schedule, a

6. Decision on questions as to disqualification on ground of 
defection.—(1) If any question arises as to whether a member of a House has 
become subject to disqualification under this Schedule, the question shall be 
referred for the decision of the Chairman or, as the case may be, the Speaker of

Provided that where the question which has arisen is as to whether the 
Chairman or the Speaker of a House has become subject to such disqualification, 
the question shall be referred for the decision of such member of the House as the 
House may elect in this behalf and his decision shall be final. 
(2) All proceedings under sub-paragraph (1) of this paragraph in relation 
to any question as to disqualification of a member of a House under this Schedule 
shall be deemed to be proceedings in Parliament within the meaning of article 
122 or, as the case may be, proceedings in the Legislature of a State within the 
meaning of article 212.

THE REPUBLIC OF INDIA AND THE GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S 
REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH CONCERNING THE DEMARCATION OF 
THE LAND BOUNDARY BETWEEN INDIA AND BANGLADESH AND 
RELATED MATTERS DATED THE 16TH DAY OF MAY, 1974 
Article 1 (12): ENCLAVES 
The Indian enclaves in Bangladesh and the Bangladesh enclaves in India 
should be exchanged expeditiously, excepting the enclaves mentioned in paragraph 
14 without claim to compensation for the additional area going to Bangladesh. 
Article 2: 
The Governments of India and Bangladesh agree that territories in adverse 
possession in areas already demarcated in respect of which boundary strip maps 
are already prepared, shall be exchanged within six months of the signing of the 
boundary strip maps by the plenipotentiaries. They may sign the relevant maps 
as early as possible as and in any case not later than the 31st December, 1974. 
Early measures may be taken to print maps in respect of other areas where 
demarcation has already taken place. These should be printed by the 31st May, 
1975 and signed by the plenipotentiaries thereafter in order that the exchange of 
adversely held possessions in these areas may take place by the 31st December, 
1975. In sectors still to be demar

boundary strip maps.

title: Definitions: Consumer, Defect, Deficiency, and Unfair Trade Practice
text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2:
(7) 'consumer' means any person who buys any goods or hires or avails of any services for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, including offline and online transactions through electronic means, but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose.
(10) 'defect' means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force.
(11) 'deficiency' means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law or in pursuance of a contract.
(47) 'unfair trade practice' includes promoting sale by misleading advertisements, false warranty claims, or refusing refund for defective goods.

title: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA): False Advertisements and Product Recall
part: Chapter III - Central Consumer Protection Authority
text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Chapter III (CCPA Regulatory Enforcement):
Section 10 establishes the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices, and false or misleading advertisements.
Section 18 & 21: The Central Authority has the power to recall goods or withdraw services which are dangerous, hazardous, or unsafe; reimburse the price of goods or services so recalled to purchasers; and discontinue practices which are unfair.
The CCPA may impose a penalty up to ten lakh rupees on a manufacturer or endorser for false or misleading advertisements, and up to fifty lakh rupees for subsequent violations, and prohibit the endorser from endorsing any product for up to one year.

title: Jurisdiction and Procedure for Filing Complaint before District Consumer Commission (e-Daakhil)
part: Chapter IV - Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Sections 34 & 35:
Section 34 (Pecuniary Jurisdiction): Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021, the District Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees (₹50,00,000). [Note: Section 34(1) of the parent 2019 Act originally specified up to ₹1 Crore, but was amended downwards by the 2021 Rules]. A complaint may be filed in the District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the complainant resides or personally works for gain, or where the opposite party works or carries on business.
Section 35: A complaint may be filed with a District Commission by the consumer, any recognized consumer association, or electronically via the e-Daakhil portal or National Consumer Helpline (NCH).

title: Admissibility of Consumer Complaint within 21 Days and Laboratory Testing Procedure
part: Chapter IV - Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Sections 36 & 38:
Section 36: On receipt of a complaint, the District Commission shall decide the admissibility of the complaint within twenty-one days from the date on which the complaint was filed. If not decided within 21 days, it is deemed admitted.
Section 38: Procedure on admission: The Commission refers a copy of the admitted complaint to the opposite party directing them to give their version within thirty days (extendable by 15 days). Where the defect cannot be determined without analysis, the Commission shall obtain a sample from the complainant, seal it, and refer it to an appropriate laboratory with directions to report findings within forty-five days.

title: Findings and Orders of the District Commission: Replacement, Refund, and Compensation
part: Chapter IV - Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission

title: Appellate Hierarchy: State Commission, National Commission (NCDRC), and Supreme Court
part: Chapter IV - Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Sections 41, 47 & 58 (Appeals & Higher Commissions):
Section 41: Any person aggrieved by an order of the District Commission may prefer an appeal to the State Commission within forty-five days from the date of the order, provided 50% of the awarded amount is deposited.
Section 47: State Commission has original jurisdiction for claims exceeding ₹50 Lakh up to ₹2 Crore (under 2021 Rules), and appellate jurisdiction over all District Commissions in the State.
Section 58: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has jurisdiction for claims exceeding ₹2 Crore, and appellate jurisdiction over State Commissions. An appeal against NCDRC lies directly before the Supreme Court under Section 67 within thirty days.

title: Product Liability Actions against Manufacturers, Service Providers, and Sellers
text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Chapter VI (Product Liability):
A product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer or a product service provider or a product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused to him on account of a defective product.
A product manufacturer shall be liable if the product contains a manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation from manufacturing specifications, or does not conform to an express warranty.
A product service provider shall be liable where the service was deficient, faulty, or where there was negligence or withholding of adequate instructions and warnings.

title: When Police May Arrest Without Warrant & Safeguards (Replacing CrPC 41)
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 35 (replacing CrPC Section 41):
(1) Any police officer may without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, arrest any person who commits, in the presence of a police officer, a cognizable offence, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made or credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years, provided conditions regarding satisfaction of necessity of arrest (preventing further offences, tampering with evidence, absconding) are recorded in writing.
(2) No arrest shall be made without prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police in offences punishable with less than three years if the accused is an infirm or aged person.

title: Right of Arrested Person to Consult Advocate during Interrogation and Mandatory 24-Hour Magistrate Production
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Sections 38 & 58:
Section 38 (replacing CrPC Section 41D): When any person is arrested and interrogated by the police, he shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation.
Section 58 (replacing CrPC Section 57): No police officer shall detain in custody a person arrested without warrant for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable, and such period shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 187, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court. Detention exceeding 24 hours without magisterial remand constitutes unlawful detention actionable by a Writ of Habeas Corpus under Article 226/32 of the Constitution.

title: Designated Police Officer in Every District and Public Display of Arrested Persons
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Sections 37 & 40 (Custodial Transparency Safeguards):
Section 37: The State Government shall establish a police control room in every district and at the state level. In every district and in every police station, a designated police officer not below the rank of Assistant Sub-Inspector shall be responsible for maintaining information regarding all arrested persons, the offences charged, and the name and designation of the arresting police officer.
Section 40: The names and details of all arrested persons and the offences for which they are arrested shall be prominently displayed outside the police control room in the district and online on digital police portals.

title: Search of Arrested Person, Female Search by Female Officer, and Mandatory Medical Examination
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Sections 47 & 53:
Section 47 (replacing CrPC Section 51): Whenever a person is arrested by a police officer, the police officer may search such person and place in safe custody all articles other than necessary wearing apparel. Whenever it is necessary to cause a female to be searched, the search shall be made by another female with strict regard to decency.
Section 53 (replacing CrPC Section 54): When any person is arrested, he shall be examined by a registered medical practitioner promptly after the arrest. A full medical examination report recording any pre-existing injuries, wounds, or marks of violence shall be prepared, and a copy of such report shall be furnished to the arrested person or their nominated person.

title: Registration of First Information Report (FIR), Zero FIR, and e-FIR Mandate
part: Chapter XIII - Information to the Police and Their Powers to Investigate
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173 (replacing CrPC Section 154):
(1) Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant.
Zero FIR Mandate: Information may be given irrespective of the area where the offence was committed; such information shall be registered as a Zero FIR and transferred to the police station having territorial jurisdiction.
e-FIR: Information may be given electronically (e-FIR), which shall be taken on record upon being signed by the person giving it within three days.
A copy of the information recorded shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant.

title: Mandatory Forensic Investigation for Heinous Offences and Videography of Search
part: Chapter XIII - Information to the Police and Their Powers to Investigate
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176(3) (Forensic Mandate):
On receipt of every information relating to the commission of an offence which is punishable for seven years or more, the officer in charge of a police station shall cause the forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence, and shall cause other evidence to be collected. The process of conducting search of a place or seizure of any property and preparation of list of all things seized shall be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably mobile phone, and forwarded without delay to the District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate.

title: Police Custody vs. Judicial Custody and Default Statutory Bail Timelines (60/90 Days)
part: Chapter XIII - Information to the Police and Their Powers to Investigate
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187 (replacing CrPC Section 167):
Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours: The Magistrate may authorize detention of the accused in custody for a term not exceeding fifteen days on the whole, or in parts, during the initial forty or sixty days.
Default Bail Mandate: The Magistrate cannot authorize detention beyond ninety days where the investigation relates to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of not less than ten years, and sixty days for any other offence.
On the expiry of the said period of 90 or 60 days, the accused person shall be released on bail if he is prepared to and does furnish bail.

title: Bail Provisions: Undertrials (Sec 479), Regular Bail in Custody (Sec 480 & 483), and Anticipatory Bail (Sec 482)
part: Chapter XXXV - Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Chapter XXXV (Bail Provisions):
Section 479 (replacing CrPC Section 436A): Maximum period for which an undertrial prisoner can be detained: where a person has, during investigation, inquiry or trial, undergone detention for up to one-half of the maximum imprisonment period, he shall be released on bail. First-time offenders (never previously convicted) shall be released on bail after undergoing detention for up to one-third.
Section 480 & 483 (replacing CrPC Sections 437 & 439 - Regular Custody Bail): When any person accused of or suspected of the commission of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained in custody, regular bail may be granted by the Magistrate (Section 480) or by the High Court or Court of Session (Section 483).
Section 482 (replacing CrPC Section 438 - Anticipatory Bail): Direction for grant of bail to a person apprehending arrest may be issued by the High Court or the Court of Session before the arrest takes place.

title: Right of Private Defence of Body and Property (Replacing IPC 96-106)
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Sections 35 to 44:
Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence. Every person has a right to defend his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body; and the property of himself or of any other person against theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass.
Section 38: The right of private defence of the body extends to causing death if the offence occasions reasonable apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, unnatural lust, or kidnapping. The right in no case extends to inflicting more harm than is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.

title: Offences Against Women: Rape, Punishment, and Sexual Intercourse by Deceitful Means
part: Chapter V - Offences Against Women and Children
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Sections 63 to 69:
Section 63 & 64 (replacing IPC 375/376): Defines rape and prescribes rigorous imprisonment for not less than ten years which may extend to life imprisonment, and fine.
Section 69 (New Provision - Sexual Intercourse by Deceitful Means): Whoever, by deceitful means or by making promise to marry to a woman without any intention of fulfilling the same, and has sexual intercourse with her, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine. Deceitful means include false promise of employment or promotion, or fictitious marriage.

title: Assault on Woman to Outrage Modesty, Stalking, and Sexual Harassment (Replacing IPC 354, 354D, 509)
part: Chapter V - Offences Against Women and Children
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Sections 74 to 79:
Section 74 (replacing IPC 354): Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty, shall be punished with imprisonment of not less than one year up to five years and fine.
Section 78 (replacing IPC 354D): Stalking: Any man who follows a woman and contacts, or attempts to contact such woman to foster personal interaction repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest; or monitors the use by a woman of internet, email or electronic communication, commits stalking, punishable up to three years (first conviction) and five years (second conviction).
Section 79 (replacing IPC 509): Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman, punishable up to three years.

title: Offences Affecting Life and Personal Safety: Murder, Hurt, and Grievous Hurt
part: Chapter VI - Offences Affecting the Human Body
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) (replacing Indian Penal Code 1860):
Section 103 (replacing IPC 302): Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
Section 115 (replacing IPC 323): Voluntarily causing hurt punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.
Section 118 (replacing IPC 326): Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years and fine.

title: Causing Death by Negligence, Hit-and-Run Rash Driving, and Medical Negligence
part: Chapter VI - Offences Affecting the Human Body
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106 (replacing IPC 304A):
(1) Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment up to two years and fine.
(2) Hit-and-Run Provision: Whoever causes the death of any person by rash and negligent driving of vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

title: Offences Against Property: Theft, Cheating, and Dishonest Inducement
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) (replacing Indian Penal Code 1860):
Section 303 (replacing IPC 378/379): Whoever intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property, commits theft. Punishable with imprisonment up to three years or fine or community service.
Section 318 (replacing IPC 415/420): Cheating: Whoever by deceiving any person fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property, commits cheating. Punishable with imprisonment extending to seven years and fine.

title: Criminal Intimidation and Extortion (Replacing IPC 503 & 506)
part: Chapter XVIII - Offences Affecting the Human Body
text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351 (replacing IPC 503/506):
Whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation. Punishable with imprisonment up to two years or fine; and if threat be to cause death or grievous hurt, with imprisonment up to seven years.

title: Right to Information: Filing Application and Mandatory 48-Hour Life/Liberty Timelines
part: Chapter II - Right to Information and Obligations of Public Authorities
text:
Right to Information Act, 2005 - Sections 3, 6 & 7:
Section 3: Subject to the provisions of this Act, all citizens shall have the right to information held by public authorities.
Section 6: A person who desires to obtain any information shall make a request in writing or through electronic means in English or Hindi or in the official language of the area, accompanying prescribed fee of ₹10.
Section 7: The Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) or State Public Information Officer (SPIO) shall provide information or reject the request as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of the receipt of the request.
Provided that where the information sought for concerns the life or liberty of a person, the same shall be provided within forty-eight hours of receipt.

title: Exemption from Disclosure of Information and Public Interest Override
part: Chapter II - Right to Information and Obligations of Public Authorities
text:
Right to Information Act, 2005 - Section 8 (Statutory Exemptions):
Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, there shall be no obligation to give any citizen information disclosure of which would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, or lead to incitement of an offence; information expressly forbidden by court of law; commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property; or information which relates to personal information the disclosure of which has no relationship to any public activity or interest.
Public Interest Override: A public authority may allow access to information if public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests.

title: First Appeal, Second Appeal to Information Commission, and CPIO Penalties
text:
Right to Information Act, 2005 - Sections 19 & 20:
Section 19: Any person who does not receive a decision within thirty days or is aggrieved by a decision of the CPIO/SPIO may within thirty days prefer a First Appeal to such officer who is senior in rank to the CPIO.
A Second Appeal against the decision of the first appellate authority lies within ninety days to the Central Information Commission (CIC) or State Information Commission (SIC).
Section 20: Where the Information Commission finds that the CPIO has without reasonable cause refused to receive an application, delayed furnishing information, or knowingly gave incorrect information, it shall impose a penalty of ₹250 per day until information is furnished, up to a maximum of ₹25,000.

article_number: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
title: Golden Triangle (Articles 14, 19, 21) & Just, Fair and Reasonable Procedure
part: Supreme Court Landmark Precedent (7-Judge Constitutional Bench)
provisions: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
text:
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248 (Supreme Court of India):
The 7-judge Constitution Bench held that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, oppressive, or fanciful; it must be 'just, fair, and reasonable', incorporating the principles of natural justice.
The Court established the doctrine of the Golden Triangle, holding that Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Freedoms), and 21 (Life and Liberty) are not water-tight compartments but form an interconnected tapestry of fundamental rights. Any law depriving a citizen of personal liberty must satisfy the tests of Article 14, 19, and 21 simultaneously. The right to travel abroad is an integral component of personal liberty.
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

article_number: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
title: Mandatory Safeguards Against Custodial Torture and Arrest Guidelines
provisions: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
text:
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416 (Supreme Court of India):
The Supreme Court laid down 11 mandatory guidelines to prevent custodial violence, wrongful police detention, and deaths in police custody:
1. Police personnel carrying out arrest must bear accurate, visible, and clear identification with name tags.
2. An arrest memo must be prepared at the time of arrest, witnessed by at least one family member or respectable citizen, and counter-signed by the arrestee.
3. The arrestee has the right to have a friend or relative informed of the arrest and place of custody within 8 to 12 hours.
4. An inspection memo must be prepared recording all pre-existing injuries on the arrestee.
5. The arrestee must undergo a medical examination by a trained doctor every 48 hours during detention.
6. The arrestee is entitled to meet and consult with their lawyer during interrogation.
Failure to comply with these requirements renders the police officer liable for contempt of court and departmental action.
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

article_number: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
title: Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right under Article 21
part: Supreme Court Landmark Precedent (9-Judge Constitutional Bench)
provisions: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
text:
Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India):
A unanimous 9-judge Constitution Bench held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected intrinsically under Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
Privacy encompasses informational privacy, bodily autonomy, and spatial privacy. Any state encroachment or surveillance on privacy must satisfy the three-fold proportionality test: (1) Legality (existence of an enacted law), (2) Legitimate state aim/need, and (3) Proportionality (rational nexus between means adopted and object sought to be achieved with least restrictive measures).
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

article_number: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
title: Decriminalization of Consensual Relations and Constitutional Morality
part: Supreme Court Landmark Precedent (5-Judge Constitutional Bench)
provisions: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
text:
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) 10 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India):
A 5-judge Constitution Bench struck down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code to the extent that it criminalized consensual sexual acts between adults in private. The Court held that sexual orientation is an inherent facet of human dignity, identity, and personal liberty under Article 21, and that discrimination on grounds of sex under Article 15 includes discrimination based on sexual orientation.
The Court reaffirmed that constitutional morality must always prevail over majoritarian public morality.
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

title: Guidelines Against Workplace Sexual Harassment under Articles 14, 19, 21
text:
Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 6 SCC 241 (Supreme Court of India):
The Supreme Court formulated the binding Vishaka Guidelines to prevent sexual harassment of women at the workplace, holding that workplace sexual harassment violates the fundamental rights to gender equality (Article 14), non-discrimination (Article 15), right to practice any profession (Article 19(1)(g)), and the right to life and dignity (Article 21).
The Court held that international conventions (CEDAW) must be read into domestic fundamental rights in the absence of enacted legislation, laying the statutory foundation for the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act).
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

article_number: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014)
title: Mandatory Notice under Section 41A and Safeguards Against Routine Arrests
provisions: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
text:
Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273 (Supreme Court of India):
The Supreme Court held that arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom and casts scars forever. Police officers shall not arrest an accused unnecessarily, and Magistrates shall not authorize detention casually and mechanically.
For offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, police must serve a notice of appearance under Section 41A (now BNSS 35(3)) within two weeks of receipt of complaint. Arrest can only be made if the accused fails to comply with terms of notice or if police satisfy the Magistrate with recorded reasons that arrest is necessary. Failure of police officers to comply renders them liable for departmental action and contempt of court.
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

article_number: Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2014)
title: Mandatory Registration of FIR in Cognizable Offences
part: Supreme Court Landmark Precedent (5-Judge Constitutional Bench)
provisions: Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P.
text:
Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2014) 2 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India):
A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence, and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation.
If the information does not disclose a cognizable offence but indicates the necessity for an inquiry, a preliminary inquiry may be conducted only to ascertain whether cognizable offence is disclosed or not, within seven days. Action must be taken against erring officers who do not register FIR if information received by them discloses a cognizable offence.
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent

article_number: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
title: Freedom of Speech Online and Striking Down of Section 66A IT Act
provisions: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
text:
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India):
The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in its entirety, holding it unconstitutional and an arbitrary infringement of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
The Court distinguished between 'discussion', 'advocacy', and 'incitement', ruling that mere advocacy or discussion of a cause, howsoever unpopular, is the heartbeat of democracy and cannot be prohibited unless it reaches the level of clear incitement to violence. The vague and overbroad terms like 'offensive' or 'annoying' created a chilling effect on legitimate speech.
source: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedent
